column2: How does gastric rotation explain the positions of the vagal trunks?
column3: Rotation around the longitudinal axis moves the stomach's left side anteriorly and its right side posteriorly, which explains the anterior and posterior positions of the vagal trunks.

column2: How does duodenal atresia arise, and why does the level of obstruction relative to the bile-duct opening matter?
column3: The duodenal epithelium temporarily occludes the lumen, and failed recanalisation produces stenosis or atresia; obstruction proximal or distal to the bile-duct opening changes the character of vomiting.

column2: What distinguishes the developmental mechanisms of pancreas divisum and annular pancreas?
column3: Pancreas divisum results when the ventral and dorsal buds fail to fuse after duodenal rotation, whereas bifid ventral tissue encircling the duodenum forms annular pancreas and can obstruct it.

column2: Why does the midgut herniate into the umbilical cord, and how does it rotate?
column3: Rapid elongation with limited abdominal space causes physiological herniation; the loop rotates about the superior mesenteric artery counterclockwise, ninety degrees while herniated and 180 on return, about 270 in total.

column2: Why does intestinal malrotation predispose to volvulus?
column3: Abnormal rotation and fixation leave an abnormal mesenteric base, which predisposes to volvulus or obstructing peritoneal bands.

column2: What distinguishes omphalocele from gastroschisis in mechanism and covering?
column3: Omphalocele is failure of herniated bowel to return and is covered by membrane at the cord base, often with other anomalies; gastroschisis is a paraumbilical wall defect with uncovered bowel and a different association pattern.

column2: How does abnormal cloacal partition produce anorectal malformations with fistulas?
column3: The urorectal septum normally divides the cloaca into anorectal canal and urogenital sinus before the cloacal membrane breaks down; abnormal partition or membrane persistence leaves malformations and fistulas to urinary or genital tracts.

column2: Why does the pectinate line predict the epithelium, blood supply, venous and lymphatic drainage, and sensory innervation of the anal canal?
column3: It marks the junction between the endodermal upper canal, supplied by inferior mesenteric circulation, and the ectodermal proctodeum below, supplied by internal iliac branches.

column2: Why does failed migration of enteric neural crest cause functional obstruction with proximal dilation?
column3: Enteric neural crest must migrate along the whole gut; if it fails distally, the bowel is left aganglionic, producing functional obstruction and dilation proximal to it.

column2: Why is the diaphragm supplied by the phrenic nerves, and why are most congenital defects posterolateral?
column3: Its motor innervation follows cervical myoblasts through the phrenic nerves, and incomplete pleuroperitoneal closure most often leaves a posterolateral defect through which abdominal organs enter the thorax.

column2: What distinguishes the derivatives of the ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme, and what follows failed induction?
column3: The ureteric bud forms ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts, while metanephric mesenchyme forms nephrons from Bowman's capsule to distal tubule; failed reciprocal induction causes renal agenesis.

column2: Why does a horseshoe kidney lie lower than normal kidneys?
column3: Kidneys begin in the pelvis and appear to ascend; when the lower poles fuse, the ascent of the fused kidney is arrested beneath the inferior mesenteric artery.

column2: How do Sertoli and Leydig cell hormones determine which genital ducts and structures develop in the male?

column2: How do the apical ectodermal ridge and zone of polarising activity pattern the limb?
column3: The apical ectodermal ridge maintains proximal-to-distal outgrowth through fibroblast growth factors, while the posterior zone of polarising activity patterns the thumb-to-little-finger axis through sonic hedgehog.
